summary: Specifies how to use the AES-CCM and AES-GCM authenticated encryption algorithms with the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is a standard way of wrapping a digital message so that only the intended recipient can open it. This document says how to protect such a message with AES, the standard encryption cipher, in two modes called CCM and GCM, which encrypt the message and check that it was not altered at the same time.

questions: how to use aes-gcm in cms
what is cms authenticated enveloped data
subtitle: How to plug the AES-CCM and AES-GCM authenticated encryption modes into CMS authenticated-enveloped data.

tldr.problem: The CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type needs a content-authenticated-encryption algorithm, and the two AES modes need agreed identifiers, parameters and usage rules if different implementations are to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns an object identifier for each AES key size and mode, defines the CCMParameters and GCMParameters structures that carry a nonce and a tag length, and requires automated key management so that a nonce and key are never reused.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can encrypt and authenticate CMS content together, in an interoperable way, provided each content is protected with a fresh key and a fresh nonce.

today: RFC 5084 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the specification for using AES-CCM and AES-GCM with the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
This document specifies the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard-Counter with Cipher Block Chaining-Message Authentication Code (AES-CCM) and AES-Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) authenticated encryption algorithms as the content-authenticated-encryption algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) RFC 3852 authenticated-enveloped-data content type, defined in RFC 5083.

AES is the block cipher selected by the National Institute for Standards and Technology from the Rijndael algorithm developed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. NIST chose it because it combines security, performance, efficiency, ease of implementation and flexibility, and because it performs well in both hardware and software across a wide range of computing environments. Its very low memory requirements make it well suited to restricted-space environments. AES specifies three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits.

CMS values are generated using ASN.1, which uses the Basic Encoding Rules and the Distinguished Encoding Rules. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHOULD and MAY in this document carry the meanings given in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is a standard way of wrapping a digital message so that only the intended recipient can open it. This document says how to protect such a message with AES, the standard encryption cipher, using two modes called CCM and GCM that encrypt the message and check it for damage at the same time.

sections.title: AES-CCM: Encryption and Checking Together
sections.content:
The Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode of operation is specified in RFC 3610. CCM is a generic authenticated encryption block cipher mode. It is defined for use with any 128-bit block cipher, but in this document it is used with the AES block cipher.

AES-CCM has four inputs: an AES key, a nonce, a plaintext, and optional additional authenticated data (AAD). It generates two outputs: a ciphertext and a message authentication code, also called an authentication tag.

The nonce is generated by the party performing the authenticated encryption operation. Within the scope of any authenticated-encryption key, the nonce value MUST be unique. That is, the set of nonce values used with any given key MUST NOT contain any duplicate values. Using the same nonce for two different messages encrypted with the same key destroys the security properties.

AAD is authenticated but not encrypted, so it is not included in the AES-CCM output. It can be used to authenticate plaintext packet headers. In the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type, the authenticated attributes comprise the AAD.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-CCM takes a key, a nonce, the message and optionally some extra data. It gives back scrambled text and a short tag that shows the text was not altered. The extra data is covered by the tag but stays readable, so it can carry things like packet headers.

sections.title: AES-GCM: The Same Inputs, a Different Mixing
sections.content:
The Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is specified in a NIST Special Publication. GCM is a generic authenticated encryption block cipher mode. It is defined for use with any 128-bit block cipher, but in this document it is used with the AES block cipher.

AES-GCM has four inputs: an AES key, an initialization vector (IV), a plaintext content, and optional additional authenticated data (AAD). It generates two outputs: a ciphertext and a message authentication code, also called an authentication tag. To have a common set of terms for AES-CCM and AES-GCM, the AES-GCM IV is referred to as a nonce in the remainder of this document.

The nonce is generated by the party performing the authenticated encryption operation. Within the scope of any authenticated-encryption key, the nonce value MUST be unique. Using the same nonce for two different messages encrypted with the same key destroys the security properties.

AAD is authenticated but not encrypted, so it is not included in the AES-GCM output. It can be used to authenticate plaintext packet headers. In the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type, the authenticated attributes comprise the AAD.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-GCM works the same way from the outside as AES-CCM: it takes a key, a nonce, the message and optionally extra data, and returns scrambled text plus a tag that shows the text was not altered. The document calls the GCM initialization vector a nonce, so both modes use the same word for it.

sections.title: Automated Key Management
sections.content:
The reuse of an AES-CCM or AES-GCM nonce and key combination destroys the security guarantees. As a result, it can be extremely difficult to use AES-CCM or AES-GCM securely when using statically configured keys. For safety's sake, implementations MUST use an automated key management system.

The CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type supports four general key management techniques. Under key transport, the content-authenticated-encryption key is encrypted in the recipient's public key. Under key agreement, the recipient's public key and the sender's private key are used to generate a pairwise symmetric key, and the content-authenticated-encryption key is encrypted in that pairwise symmetric key. Under symmetric key-encryption keys, the content-authenticated-encryption key is encrypted in a previously distributed symmetric key-encryption key. Under passwords, the content-authenticated-encryption key is encrypted in a key-encryption key that is derived from a password or other shared secret value.

All four of these techniques meet the automated key management system requirement as long as a fresh content-authenticated-encryption key is generated for the protection of each content. Some of them use one key-encryption key to encrypt more than one content-authenticated-encryption key during the system life cycle; as long as a fresh content-authenticated-encryption key is used each time, the two modes can be used safely with the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type.

CMS supports other key management techniques, listed in Section 6.2.5 of RFC 3852. Since the properties of those techniques are unknown, the RFC makes no statement about whether they meet the automated key management system requirement. Designers and implementers must perform their own analysis if one of them is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The fastest way to break these modes is to use the same key and nonce twice. So the document insists that keys come from an automated key management system and that each message gets a fresh key. It lists four ways to deliver that key: inside the recipient's public key, agreed with the recipient, wrapped in a symmetric key, or wrapped in a key derived from a password.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
Content-authenticated encryption algorithm identifiers are located in the AuthEnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo contentEncryptionAlgorithm field. The algorithms are used to encipher the content located in the AuthEnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo encryptedContent field and to provide the message authentication code for the AuthEnvelopedData mac field. That code gives integrity protection for both the AuthEnvelopedData authAttrs and the AuthEnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo encryptedContent.

For AES-CCM there are three algorithm identifiers, one for each AES key size: id-aes128-CCM, id-aes192-CCM and id-aes256-CCM. With all three, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and must contain a CCMParameters structure. Its aes-nonce field is an OCTET STRING of size 7 to 13, and its aes-ICVlen field gives the size of the message authentication code. Neither the plaintext content nor the optional AAD inputs need to be padded before AES-CCM is invoked.

The aes-nonce field contains 15-L octets, where L is the size of the length field. Because the normal CMS situation is for the content-authenticated-encryption key to protect a single content, L=8 is RECOMMENDED. The aes-ICVlen value MUST match the size in octets of the value in the AuthEnvelopedData mac field, and a length of 12 octets is RECOMMENDED.

For AES-GCM there are three algorithm identifiers as well: id-aes128-GCM, id-aes192-GCM and id-aes256-GCM. The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and must contain a GCMParameters structure. Its aes-nonce is the AES-GCM initialization vector and its aes-ICVlen gives the size of the message authentication code. The algorithm specification permits the nonce to have any number of bits between 1 and 2^64, but the use of OCTET STRING requires the nonce to be a multiple of 8 bits. A nonce of 12 octets can be processed more efficiently, so that length is RECOMMENDED. The aes-ICVlen value MUST again match the mac field, and 12 octets is RECOMMENDED. Neither the plaintext content nor the optional AAD inputs need to be padded before AES-GCM is invoked.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mode and key size gets its own name inside the message, so the recipient knows which algorithm to use. Next to the name go two settings: the nonce and the length of the tag. The document recommends a 12-octet tag for both modes, and a 12-octet nonce for GCM.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AES-CCM and AES-GCM make use of the AES block cipher in counter mode to provide encryption. When used properly, counter mode provides strong confidentiality. Bellare, Desai, Jokipii and Rogaway show that the privacy guarantees provided by counter mode are at least as strong as those for Cipher Block Chaining mode when using the same block cipher.

Unfortunately, it is easy to misuse counter mode. If counter block values are ever used for more than one encryption operation with the same key, then the same key stream is used to encrypt both plaintexts, and the confidentiality guarantees are voided. Fortunately, the CMS AuthEnvelopedData provides all the tools needed to avoid this, through the automated key management described in Section 2.

There are fairly generic precomputation attacks against the use of any block cipher in counter mode that allow a meet-in-the-middle attack against the key. These attacks require the creation and searching of huge tables of ciphertext associated with known plaintext and known keys. Assuming that the memory and processor resources for such an attack are available, then the theoretical strength of any block cipher in counter mode is limited to 2^(n/2) bits, where n is the number of bits in the key. The use of long keys is the best countermeasure to precomputation attacks, and an unpredictable nonce value in the counter block significantly increases the size of the table that an attacker must compute to mount a successful attack.

Implementations must randomly generate content-authenticated-encryption keys. The use of inadequate pseudo-random number generators to generate cryptographic keys can result in little or no security. An attacker may find it much easier to reproduce the PRNG environment that produced the keys and then search the resulting small set of possibilities, rather than brute-force search the whole key space. RFC 4086 offers important guidance in this area.
sections.plainLanguage: Counter mode is strong when it is used correctly and broken when it is not. If the same key and nonce are used twice, the same secret key stream is produced and the encryption collapses, which is why the document insists on automated key management and a fresh key each time. The keys must also come from a good random number generator, because a weak one lets an attacker guess its output.

viz.caption: The four key management techniques CMS supports

items.title: Key transport
items.text: The content-authenticated-encryption key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.

items.title: Key agreement
items.text: The recipient's public key and the sender's private key generate a pairwise symmetric key, which then wraps the content key.

items.title: Symmetric key-encryption keys
items.text: The content key is encrypted in a symmetric key-encryption key that was distributed earlier.

items.title: Passwords
items.text: The content key is encrypted in a key-encryption key derived from a password or other shared secret.
